title.en: Environment-led studio lighting for physically based materials

summary: Let a controlled environment carry most of the illumination, and add discrete lights only for the shaping the environment cannot supply.
objective: Metal and dielectric parts separate by their reflections rather than by their base colour, and the environment can be rotated without changing which parts read as metal.
intent_signals: how do I light a PBR model
example_prompts: Light a product so its metal and painted parts are clearly different.
Set up a neutral studio for comparing two material finishes.
Rotate the environment to find a reading angle for a curved surface.
negative_signals: quantitative colour encoding must not be shaded
not_for: Views where colour carries data and any shading would corrupt the reading.
Outdoor scenes whose whole point is a directional sun and sky.

principles: In a metallic-roughness workflow the environment is the main light source for reflective materials. A metal with nothing around it to reflect has almost nothing to show, which is why isolated metal renders as dull grey.
The environment is a light, not a backdrop. Deciding what the object reflects is a lighting decision even when the environment is never visible behind the object.
Discrete lights should have a stated job: a highlight the environment cannot place, a separation rim, or a shadow that grounds the object. A light without a job usually flattens the result.

Roughness is what turns a light into a shape. A narrow highlight reads as polish, a broad one reads as satin, and reading the difference requires an environment with real variation rather than a uniform grey dome.
The same environment applied to every object in a comparison is what makes the comparison fair. Changing the environment between variants changes the conclusion.
implementation: Choose the environment first and state what it represents: a soft box array, an interior, an open sky. Give it real large-scale variation, since a perfectly uniform environment removes the reflections that read as material.

Apply the environment at the scene level so all physically based materials receive it consistently, and be aware that a material carrying its own explicit environment map will not be overridden by the scene-level setting.
Control environment brightness through its own intensity, and control the visible backdrop separately, so the lighting can be adjusted without changing what the viewer sees behind the object.
Rotate the environment to place its bright regions where the object needs a highlight; this is usually a faster and more reversible control than moving several discrete lights.
Add at most a small number of named discrete lights, each with a written purpose, and check whether removing each one changes anything the record cares about.

Give the object light from below by a named mechanism rather than by assuming a floor will bounce it: an environment contribution, a baked or global-illumination solution, or an explicit weak fill light. A direct-light rasteriser produces no bounce from an ordinary visible floor, and a floating object with nothing from below reads as a cut-out.
Keep the environment fixed while material variants are being judged, and change one thing at a time.
observable_checks: Turning the object shows a moving highlight whose width matches the roughness the record assigns to each part.
A metal part and a painted part at the same base colour are still distinguishable, and remain distinguishable when the environment is rotated.
Removing each named discrete light produces a visible loss the record can name; a light whose removal changes nothing is not doing the job it claims.
Every object in a comparison is under the same environment, with the same intensity and rotation.
Raising environment intensity brightens the reflections and the diffuse response together, and does not silently change the visible backdrop unless that was intended.

creative_affordances: The environment can be invented, stylised or coloured for narrative purposes; it does not have to be a photographic studio.
Strong single-source lighting, deep shadow and high-contrast staging remain available choices when the record states the intent.
known_limits: Using a physically based material model and an environment does not make a render photometrically accurate; brightness units, exposure and display transform all remain open decisions.
The scene-level environment behaviour cited here is documented for one renderer and does not describe how other engines resolve material-level and scene-level environments.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact or rendered result has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: In one widely used renderer a scene-level environment map is applied to all physical materials in the scene but does not overwrite an environment map already assigned on a material, environment intensity and rotation affect only that environment, and background blurriness and background intensity affect only the visible background rather than the lighting.
claims.scope: Documented scene properties of one library as of the access date. They describe where environment lighting is resolved and what the background controls do not affect; they make no photometric claim.

claims.statement: In the glTF 2.0 metallic-roughness model the base colour is interpreted differently by metalness: for a metal it is the measured reflectance at normal incidence, while for a non-metal it is the reflected diffuse colour and a fixed linear value of four percent is used for normal-incidence reflectance, which cannot be specified separately.
claims.scope: Normative material-model text of the glTF 2.0 specification, read from the Khronos specification source. It defines how one parameter set is interpreted; it does not assert that any authored value matches a measured material.
